People will naturally try to fit what you're doing into a box they already know. Initial growth is a lot slower than fitting into an established category with existing market demand. It’s WAY harder to sell something that people need, but don’t think they want. That's the tax of category creation. You're not just building a product. You're building understanding. Most builders can’t stomach these tradeoffs. Or their investors won’t allow it. So they collapse back into copying competitor features and positioning in a category people already think they want. But for a Category Creator, the future is INEVITABLE. It’s only a matter of time. It’s not my first rodeo building a new category. Here are the top lessons I’ve learned: 1. Reject the premise. The World is the way it is because someone in the past decided that’s how it will be. With AI, the premise of most current business systems is flawed. 2. Focus on the outcome. 3. Be patient.

posts.full_text: Boost Hotel Bookings with 10 Essential Strategies for Q2. We’re almost done with the first quarter... 1. Go all-in on long-form video immediately. Not polished brand fluff, real storytelling. 3-5 minute videos about your property, your people, your destination. This is how you win in AI search and discoverability going forward, not 15-second clips. 2. Put your GM, owner, or leadership team on camera now. Founder-led content builds trust faster than any campaign you can pay for. If they’re not comfortable, fix that. Media training is cheaper than missed revenue. 3. Stop posting like a brochure. Nobody cares about your rooms and your pool if that’s all you show. Start telling stories about guests, staff, local culture, behind-the-scenes operations. Make people feel something. 4. Turn your destination into your biggest asset. You’re not just selling a hotel, you’re selling why someone should get on a plane. Highlight restaurants, neighborhoods, hidden gems, local personalities. Become the media company for your destination. 5. Aggressively respond to every single comment and message. This is not optional. Engagement drives reach, reach drives bookings. Most brands still post and disappear, and that’s a massive mistake. 6. Build a real content engine, not random posts. You should have clear content pillars and a weekly cadence across platforms. If your team is guessing what to post each day, you’ve already lost. 7. Partner with creators who understand storytelling, not just influencers with big numbers. If they can’t drive conversation and retention, they won’t drive revenue. Be selective and think long-term partnerships, not one-off posts. 8. Fix your LinkedIn strategy immediately. This is where decision-makers, event planners, and corporate buyers are. Your hotel should be showing thought leadership, not just job postings and press releases. 9. Capture everything. Every activation, every guest experience should be documented. If it’s not being filmed or photographed, you’re leaving content and money on the table. 10. Make your marketing accountable to revenue. If your social media team can’t tie what they’re doing back to bookings, pipeline, or brand demand, you don’t have a strategy, you have activity. The hotels that win this year aren’t the ones with the biggest budgets. They’re the ones willing to move fast, get uncomfortable, and actually change how they show up. --- If you like the way I look at the world of hospitality, let’s chat: scott@mrscotteddy.com.

posts.full_text: This is one of the most misunderstood parts of social media, especially in hospitality, and I’ve seen it play out in my own business more times than I can count. Some of the biggest clients I’ve ever signed never liked a single post. Never left a comment. Never engaged with me. If you looked at my analytics, you’d think they didn’t exist. But then one day, out of nowhere, they reach out via DM and say they’ve been following everything I’ve been doing for years. Not weeks, not months, years. And within a few conversations, we’re doing business together. That’s the silent follower, and most brands completely underestimate how powerful that audience really is. The mistake I see all the time is people obsessing over visible engagement. Likes, comments, shares. They treat those as the only signals that something is working. And if those numbers aren’t high enough, they assume the content failed. What they don’t realize is that a huge percentage of their audience is watching everything, paying attention, forming an opinion, and never touching the like button. Especially at the higher end of the market, decision makers don’t engage publicly. General managers, owners, investors, they’re not sitting there liking every post. They’re observing. They’re evaluating. They’re quietly deciding whether you’re credible enough to trust with their business. By the time they reach out, the decision is already halfway made. That completely changes how you should think about content. You’re not just creating for the people who engage. You’re creating for the people who are watching. And those are often the ones that matter most. This is why consistency matters so much more than people think. Every post is another touchpoint. Another data point. Another moment where someone who has never engaged is building a deeper understanding of who you are and what you do. You don’t see it happening, but it’s happening. It also means you need to stop judging your content purely on surface-level metrics. Engagement is important, but it’s not the full picture. There’s a whole layer of influence that isn’t visible, and that’s where a lot of real business actually comes from. From a practical standpoint, this should push you to go deeper with your content, not safer. The silent followers aren’t converting because of generic posts. They’re converting because over time, you’ve shown expertise, consistency, and a clear point of view. You’ve given them enough confidence to reach out without ever needing to interact publicly. So when you feel like a post didn’t perform because it didn’t get enough likes, remember this. You have no idea who’s watching. You have no idea who’s paying attention. And you definitely don’t know who’s one or two posts away from reaching out. Because in my experience, the people who say nothing are often the ones making the biggest moves behind the scenes.

But it requires looking at your portfolio as a visibility system not a collection of individual hotel websites.

posts.full_text:
How to get your hotel recommended by AI (and what you can do starting today)

Because if AI doesn't recommend your hotel, you're invisible.

Not on Google. Not on OTAs. Invisible at the exact moment a guest is ready to book. And that shift happened faster in the last 12 months than in the last decade.

Guests aren't browsing anymore. They're asking:
"Best design hotel in Barcelona for couples."
"Luxury safari lodge with strong wellness offering."
"Top beachfront hotel in Dubai for a long weekend."

AI responds with a shortlist. Not ten blue links. Not endless scrolling. A shortlist. If you're not on it, you don't exist in that decision.

So how do hotels get recommended?

1️⃣ Say Something Worth Repeating
AI favours insight. Not "luxury, world-class, exceptional." Not recycled amenities. Specific positioning. Clear differentiation. A perspective that feels owned. If your copy could belong to any hotel, AI won't prioritise it.

2️⃣ Control the Narrative
AI can assist with creation. But strategy must be human. Your tone. Your structure. Your facts. Your proof. Consistency across website, press, social, listings. Fragmented messaging weakens trust signals.

3️⃣ Stay Fresh
Updated pages build credibility. Refined FAQs. Current experiences. Evolving offers. Dormant content fades. Active brands surface.

Hotels that appear consistently in AI answers follow a simple cycle:
→ Identify high-intent guest questions
→ Create structured, specific content
→ Audit where AI mentions you
→ Align messaging across every platform
→ Refine and repeat

In practice, that means:
• Answer real guest questions clearly
• Update core pages quarterly
• Earn mentions on credible third-party sites
• Structure experiences in a machine-readable way
• Track AI visibility, not just website traffic

The hotels building trust now become the ones AI keeps recommending. Everyone else will be reacting later.

BOOK
The Art of Gathering by Priya Parker. Design gatherings around transformation, not logistics. The hotels that understand this move up the value chain.

TREND
Travel spend is polarising. Luxury remains comparatively stable. Mid-market tightens. Budget becomes more competitive. The middle narrows. Brands either justify a premium or compete on efficiency. Anything unclear gets squeezed.

If you're in hospitality right now, the question isn't growth. I would say it's positioning. Which side of the divide are you on? 👇

posts.full_text:
Stop giving guests what you think they want. Start giving them what they actually value. And this is why segmenting your audience and aligning with what they want and are interested in most is no longer optional.

Here are the 7 shifts shaping guest expectations (and why they matter):

From perks → to presence
Champagne on arrival is nice, okay I'll admit it. But what guests really value is how they feel while they're with you. It's about presence; the sense that a hotel sees them, anticipates their needs and makes space for them to be in the moment.

From amenities → to rituals
Hotels have long sold access to gyms, spas and pools. Now the question is: what do guests do there? A morning plunge, a tea ritual, an evening wind-down routine; these daily anchors turn amenities into meaningful moments that guests carry home with them.

From check-in/out → to continuous journey
The stay doesn't start at the front desk anymore. It begins the moment a guest searches, books, or receives a pre-arrival message. And it doesn't end at checkout: it continues in post stay follow-ups, loyalty touch points and digital connections that keep the relationship alive.

From logos → to low-key design
Luxury today whispers. I love the expression 'quiet luxury'. Guests are drawn to natural textures and spaces that feel authentic to place not branded walls shouting status. The emphasis is on subtlety, restraint and design that is authentic and lets the environment breathe.

From "all you can eat" → to personalised nourishment
The buffet era is fading. ( Sorry I know I'll get a lil hate for this ;) ) Guests expect food designed around health, preferences and sometimes even their biological data. From plant-based fine dining to nutritionist-led menus, the future of F&B is deeply personal and deeply intentional.

From transactions → to transformations
A hotel stay isn't just about service standards. It's about what changes in the guest: Did they leave restored, inspired, more themselves than when they arrived? Hospitality becomes not just a transaction but a catalyst for growth, healing, or transformation.

From sustainability → to regeneration
It's no longer enough to 'do less harm.' Guests are demanding hotels contribute to positive impact: restoring ecosystems, uplifting local communities, and leaving destinations better than they were found. Regeneration is the new benchmark.

Hospitality in 2025 isn't about things. It's about meaning.

So what is your meaning? What are your guests coming for?

Yesterday we posted a job for a content marketing manager and the results/interactions have been very insightful.

Within 24 hours we had 1000 views and 300 applications with perhaps 1/3 of this looking like a good fit.

Of these applications:
- 5 messaged me directly to share enthusiasm about their application
- 3 asked me what the job description was and expectations for the role (despite it being posted)
- 4 people emailed their cv directly
- 2 sent videos (1 was a generic video cv)

As step one of the short recruitment process we had asked for candidates to submit a brief video sharing why they want to work for FDS and what we can expect from them. Only 2 emailed to say they would be sending their video… the rest?

Either didn't read the recruitment process clearly detailed at the bottom of the posting, or didn't yet have time or inclination to create a video and of course some may not even want to.

Why did we do this?
- It really shows who genuinely reads the job post versus just selecting easy apply without fully understanding the role
- We can see quickly for personality fit with the company.
- It whittles out those who opt for low effort job applications vs those who present enthusiastic/ positive desire to work with us

During my corporate days I was exposed to many recruitment processes and was sat on both sides of the table. When hiring for teams we always saw the most efficient process when we had a diligent video screening.

So for anyone who has applied and hasn't send a video this is your subtle hint to please do so, especially as it gives anyone whose cv or experience may not seem a direct fit to voice over why we should consider you.

And for those who haven't used video screening what are your thoughts?

“This hotel should be recommended.”

SEO helps search engines rank your website.
GEO helps AI trust your hotel enough to recommend it.
That means working on things like:
• Clear positioning (what your hotel is known for)
• Consistent information across the internet
• Credible sources mentioning your brand
• Structured content AI can understand
Simple way to remember it:
SEO = win the ranking.
GEO = win the recommendation.
The hotels that understand this shift early will own the new discovery layer.

We flew to Dubai this week for a meeting that never happened.
Instead, we got stuck there. Here's what happened.

We arrived on Thursday for a meeting scheduled on Friday.
It got cancelled.

Our flight out was Monday, so we stayed for the weekend to 'relax' before the next leg of our trip.

Then the situation escalated.

On Saturday afternoon, explosions were heard over parts of the city.

Like many others in the city that night, we had to leave our room and take shelter.

Moments like this change how you look at hospitality.

Because when things are uncertain, what guests remember is not the design, the view or the amenities.

They remember how they were treated.

One gesture stood out.

When the team at the Palazzo Versace Dubai heard about our situation, they offered us a night at the hotel with breakfast simply as a way to help. No marketing. No publicity. Just hospitality. And it reminded me of something important about this industry. Real hospitality is not tested when everything runs smoothly. It reveals itself when things go wrong. When guests are uncertain, when plans collapse, when reassurance matters more than service standards. That's when culture shows. And in moments like these, the smallest gestures often create the strongest loyalty.

How to build a 1,000-person email list before your hotel opens its doors

Most hotels start marketing when construction is almost finished.
By then, you’re late.

Pre-opening isn’t about announcing a building.
It’s about engineering demand before the first guest arrives.

Here’s the framework:

1️⃣ Don’t market the hotel.
Market the reason someone would book it.

No one subscribes to:

“New five-star hotel opening soon.”

They subscribe to:

• A honeymoon that feels like the world paused
• A reset before burnout hits
• A birthday weekend that becomes part of their story
• A proposal location no one else knows yet
• A place to disappear for 72 hours

People don’t wake up wanting a hotel.

They wake up wanting a feeling, a change, a moment a transformation.

Your hotel is the vehicle.

2️⃣ Define 5 revenue-driving decisions

For example:

• Where to go for a private honeymoon
• Where to reset for 3–4 days
• Where to celebrate something meaningful
• Where to spend a design-led weekend
• Where to take the family without compromising on luxury

Every piece of content should ladder up to one of these.

That’s how you attract the right 1,000 subscribers not just traffic.

3️⃣ Turn vision into desire

You don’t need a finished building.

Use:

• Architectural renders
• Founder vision
• Mood boards
• Behind-the-scenes progress

Then turn them into:
• Cinematic pre-opening videos
• AI-generated lifestyle photography/ video
• Story-led room walkthroughs

But frame everything around:

“What staying here will feel like.”

Construction updates don’t build lists.
Emotional anticipation does.

4️⃣ Exchange value, not updates

No one gives their email for “news”.

They will give it for:

• Founders’ rates
• Priority booking access
• Private preview invitations
• Members-only perks
• Early access to limited suites

Scarcity and status convert.

5️⃣ Design the email journey before bookings open

An email list without a sequence is a vanity metric.

Map:

Awareness → Desire → Trust → Early Access → Priority Booking

By the time reservations open,
your first guests should already feel like insiders.

Open with 1,000 qualified subscribers and:

• Your first weeks feel like an event
• Your pricing holds

Let's reverse-engineer it.

Opening goal:
50% occupancy
ADR: $700
Average stay: 2 nights
Assume a 100-key hotel.

That equals:
50 rooms occupied per night
100 room nights per day

Step 1: How many bookings do we need?
100 room nights ÷ 2-night average stay → 50 bookings per day

Distribution mix (simplified):
50% OTA / 50% Direct
So: 25 bookings/day via OTAs / 25 bookings/day via direct channels

Step 2: What does that mean for direct traffic?
Industry-average direct website conversion rate: 1–2%
To generate 25 direct bookings/day:
At 1% conversion → 2,500 website visitors/day
At 2% conversion → 1,250 website visitors/day

That's 37,500–75,000 qualified visitors per month before and during the opening phase. And this is just for direct.

Step 3: What about OTAs?
OTAs don't remove the need for marketing. They just change where demand converts.
Most OTA demand is created upstream by: Social content / Video / Press / Paid discovery
In other words: OTAs capture demand — they don't magically create it.

Step 4: So where does the traffic come from?
1. Organic content: Short-form video / Long-form video / SEO + AI discovery
Role: Build desire and confidence before guests compare prices.

2. Paid distribution: Paid social / Retargeting / Launch-phase media burst
Role: Speed. Control. Predictability.

3. Conversion assets: Clear room pages / Strong visual storytelling / Reduced booking friction
Role: Turn interest into bookings.

Openings usually fail because demand is never quantified.
The missing piece is usually not budget — it's a clear guest journey: from discovery → confidence → booking.

How much traffic do you need?

Website build.
CRM setup.
Tracking.

That’s infrastructure.

Ads.
SEO.
Social.
PR.

That’s execution.

If you mix them together, budgets get confused and expectations get misaligned.

• A basic website

• No clear audience
• No structured content
• No AI architecture

Foundations are not decoration.

No waitlist.
No early access list.
No database.

posts.full_text:
7 Myths About Luxury Hospitality (that 2025 is proving wrong) 👇

For years, luxury hotels have been built on traditions that no longer resonate with today's travellers. Here are 7 of the biggest myths being rewritten:

❌ Work & wellness don't mix — Wellness isn't just for vacations. Guests are blending it into their daily rhythm: cold plunges before breakfast, workouts after meetings.

❌ 'Sustainable' is enough — Offsetting isn't the benchmark anymore. Regeneration is: restoring nature, uplifting communities, and leaving a place better.

❌ Buffets = abundance — What once symbolised wealth now signals waste. Guests notice.

❌ Luxury is stuffy — Rigid dress codes and formality are out. Today's luxury is effortless: built on authenticity, warmth, and comfort.

❌ More amenities = more value — A long list of features doesn't impress. Thoughtful rituals and meaningful experiences do.

❌ Luxury = loud branding — Logos, gold, noise: less is more. Quiet luxury wins.

❌ Points = loyalty — It's no longer about collecting. Loyalty now comes from being recognised, remembered, and truly cared for.

Luxury in 2025 is quieter, healthier, and more intentional.

👉 What other 'myths' about luxury hospitality do you think are ready to be broken? 👇

Not chasing the corner office. Not ready for the rocking chair. A little less interested in being impressive and a lot more interested in being useful, wise, and maybe even joyful.

posts.full_text: 2025 is the Year You Expand Your Horizons “Our task is to be defeated by ever-larger things.” - Rainer Maria Rilke You don’t know your limits until you’ve exceeded them. I’ve learned that as an entrepreneur who flirted with bankruptcy, as a blogger sharing my very personal revelations that some in my family find embarrassing, as a middlescent masquerading as an adolescent with my crude sexual jokes, and as a friend who’s willing to “go there” in my deep conversations with good friends. Heck, a year ago, I was launching a book while being on GMA and The Today Show soon to be opening our Santa Fe campus just as I was finishing 36 sessions of radiation and two years of hormone depletion therapy. If I wanted to be safe, I would have never left my crib. Rilke’s quote reminds me that it’s fine to be on the losing side of an election if you feel passionately about your cause. It’s okay to lose a court battle if you’re pursuing justice. It’s painful but beautiful to pursue someone you love who just isn’t available to you…yet. It’s nice to feel safe, but the other meaning of a safe is a bulletproof cabinet with a complex lock that no one but you can open. Maybe it’s time you came out of your protected, predictable safe and tested yourself. What if 2025 was the year you expanded your boundaries a bit? Found something big enough to be defeated by and, defiantly, came back to conquer it the same year? Scared to do it? That’s a good sign. You don’t have to do it alone. There’s a whole movement of MEA alums in 60 regional chapters around the world who are spreading their wings just like you. They and we are here to support you.

posts.full_text: I travel often globally out of passion for hospitality and in support of our industry. I am often asked where are my favorite places to visit and that is like being asked to choose your favorite child- you love them all equally for different reasons. That said, 40 years ago I experienced Kyoto, Nara and Osaka Japan for the first time on a Summer scholarship and homestay experience, one of 3 times living in Japan. That first experience profoundly changed the aperature through which I saw and experienced life and saw common human experiences through a lens vastly different from my own. It was even more meaningful because I did not grow up with much money or the ability to travel domestically much less internationally even as my parents gave us the gift of travel and experiences locally (and many roadtrips in an old school station wagon). Kyoto forever embedded itself in my heart. It still vibrates in my soul at the same frequency. It awakened and tapped into part of me that was always there— including a hospitality gene— but which had not been fully activated, much less expressed, living in the US. Those experiences and especially the year I lived in Kyoto, led to so many of the most profound and positive changes and decisions in my life, including meeting my now wife who shares a passion for Japan going back as long as myself, even as neither of us are Japanese. And perhaps, no surprise, independently, my wife has a career in our beloved travel industry as well. So many friendships, experiences and life altering growth experiences and changes all flowed from those early experiences in Japan and how it profoundly changed me for the better. After many years of planning, my wife and I finally had the opportunity this week to share our love of Japan and provide an opportunity for our kids to experience Japan for their first time. posts.full_text: A new piece I have written for ELLE magazine... "In 2025, travel is going to be about doing everything and being everywhere all at once. Or, at least, trying to. Cultural cues will be absorbed instantaneously, kickstarting our curiosity. "Paradoxically, we’ll also be seeing a hunger for ‘quiet travel’ in nature and an embracing of the joys of the mundane (think ‘supermarket tourism’) in destinations such as Oslo – a place its own tourism board playfully mocked in a quirky video campaign, whose message of: ‘I wouldn’t come here to be honest. I mean… is it even a city?’ went viral."
